# Index design: an access path that earns its cost

[← All question groups](../index.md) · `sql-index-design` · **SQL Server & Data Engineering** · Catalog level: foundation

<p>Questions come from the preserved source notes. Reframing, assessment intent, senior signals and rubrics are editorial interpretations, not verified model answers or universal interviewer expectations. Follow-ups and the combined production exercise are agent additions. Reading this bank creates no learning record, score, completion or review schedule.</p>

## Start with one representative question

[S03-Q011](#S03-Q011)

<p>What evidence would justify creating an index, and how would you decide whether to keep it after deployment?</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Choose and validate an index from a concrete workload&#x27;s access needs and maintenance costs.</p>

<ul>
<li>Trace rowstore access and distinguish the roles of index structures.</li>
<li>Justify composite key order and coverage for declared predicates and output.</li>
<li>Interpret plan/read evidence and evaluate write regressions before retaining a change.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

No catalog prerequisite. Establish the terms and scenario assumptions in the foundation questions before progressing; a published lesson is not evidence that you know them.

<p>When should an index be created? Build the decision from how indexed keys locate data, then examine the query&#x27;s access requirements. Seek, scan and lookup observations connect that model to evidence; read gains must still justify the workload&#x27;s storage and write costs.</p>

<a id="S03-Q007"></a>

### S03-Q007 · Foundation

<p>Which SQL Server index types are relevant to the workloads you know, and how would you distinguish their intended uses?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q007](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q007)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q007](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q007)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What index types are commonly used in SQL Server?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Build a useful classification rather than recite every index name. Relate an index category to the access pattern it is intended to support.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Organize index choices by workload and supported capabilities.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Establish the SQL Server version, edition and table/storage form; consult official documentation before claiming an index type is available or suitable.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Distinguishes categories using a concrete read or write pattern.</li>
<li>Separates feature availability from measured suitability for that workload.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Listing types without explaining differences or assuming every deployment supports all types.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>Which evidence would narrow the choices for a mixed transactional and reporting workload?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q010"></a>

### S03-Q010 · Mechanism

<p>Using a small example, explain how an index helps a database locate data and why the same index may not help every query.</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q010](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q010)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q010](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q010)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How does an index work conceptually?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Trace the access mechanism from a search condition to candidate rows. Connect the organization of indexed keys to the shape of the query.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Explain index behavior causally rather than by analogy alone.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Choose a conventional SQL Server rowstore index and a stated predicate. Keep conceptual access separate from the actual optimizer plan.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Walks through a concrete lookup and the data still required afterward.</li>
<li>Names a changed query or data distribution that needs a different access path.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Stopping at &#x27;like a book index&#x27; without mapping keys, candidate rows and access cost.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you check whether SQL Server actually used the path you described?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q008"></a>

### S03-Q008 · Mechanism

<p>Compare clustered and nonclustered rowstore indexes in SQL Server. How does each affect locating a requested row?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q008](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q008)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q008](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q008)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare clustered and nonclustered indexes.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Use one lookup to explain the difference in the structures and their relationship to table data. Avoid replacing the mechanism with a faster/slower ranking.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Explain the row access path and consequences of the index structure.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Limit the comparison to ordinary rowstore tables and state whether the base table is clustered or a heap; specialized index types are outside this question.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Traces a lookup from the chosen key toward the required row values.</li>
<li>Connects a key choice to storage or update cost without inventing a performance result.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Claiming one index type always wins or that physical output order replaces ORDER BY.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What changes in a nonclustered lookup when the base table is a heap?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q013"></a>

### S03-Q013 · Mechanism

<p>How do the order of columns in a composite index and the distribution of their values affect a query&#x27;s access options?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q013](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q013)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q013](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q013)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How do composite index key order and selectivity affect a query?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>A composite index has several key columns. Selectivity describes how narrowly a condition identifies data; explain its relationship to the actual predicate and ordering needs.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Reason about key order from a concrete query and data distribution.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a SQL Server rowstore example with equality/range predicates and required sorting stated. Do not assume selectivity alone determines the best key order.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Compares candidate orders against the same query&#x27;s access requirements.</li>
<li>Uses plan and read evidence to test the choice under relevant data distributions.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Applying &#x27;most selective column first&#x27; as a universal rule without examining predicates.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would the choice change when a frequent query omits one predicate?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q014"></a>

### S03-Q014 · Application

<p>What makes an index cover a particular query, and when would you consider INCLUDE columns in SQL Server?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q014](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q014)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q014](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q014)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What is a covering index and when is `INCLUDE` useful?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Relate coverage to everything the query needs, not to the table as a whole. Compare key columns and included columns for that access pattern.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Design query coverage while accounting for its storage and write costs.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Specify the query, SQL Server version and index type; verify INCLUDE capabilities and limits in official documentation. No automatic performance improvement is assumed.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Accounts for predicates, output columns and relevant ordering in the proposal.</li>
<li>Checks the access plan and workload cost before retaining the extra columns.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Including every column or claiming a covering index is best for every query.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>When would you avoid covering a query with a very wide output?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q015"></a>

### S03-Q015 · Application

<p>Explain index seek, scan and key lookup in a SQL Server execution plan. How would you decide whether the observed access is a problem?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q015](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q015)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q015](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q015)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain index seek, scan and key lookup.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Interpret what the operators do for a particular query. Evaluate the amount of work rather than label an operator good or bad from its name.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Use access operators as diagnostic evidence in context.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a stated rowstore query and actual plan where available. Separate estimates from observations and do not invent execution results.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Traces the data access and rows involved in each relevant operator.</li>
<li>Relates reads, row counts and required output to a testable change.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Assuming every seek is efficient or every scan requires an index fix.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What would you inspect if a plan uses a seek but still performs many reads?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q012"></a>

### S03-Q012 · Failure cases

<p>When could adding an index make the overall system slower, even if one query improves?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q012](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q012)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q012](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q012)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> When can an index make the system slower?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Explain a regression as a causal chain. Identify where extra work appears and which measurements distinguish it from unrelated load changes.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Diagnose an indexing trade-off at system level.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Consider a SQL Server workload containing both reads and writes. State the changed index and compare similar load conditions; no regression is assumed observed.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Connects a proposed regression to write, resource or plan effects.</li>
<li>Specifies evidence that separates competing explanations before removing the index.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Saying &#x27;too many indexes&#x27; without showing which work or constraint caused the slowdown.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you investigate a slowdown that appears only during a bulk import?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q009"></a>

### S03-Q009 · Trade-offs

<p>What benefits and costs would you assess before adding an index to a SQL Server workload?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q009](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q009)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q009](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q009)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What are the advantages and costs of indexes?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Compare the read paths helped by the index with the work introduced elsewhere. Make the unit of evaluation a workload, not one isolated SELECT.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Balance access benefits against storage, writes and maintenance.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State representative queries, update frequency and storage constraints. Benefits are hypotheses until checked with relevant measurements.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Links the proposed index to a specific access pattern and competing write load.</li>
<li>Defines before/after measurements and a condition for rejecting the index.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Counting the number of indexes as a quality measure or discussing reads alone.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you decide whether a rarely used index is still worth retaining?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q016"></a>

### S03-Q016 · Trade-offs

<p>How would you adapt an indexing strategy for a write-heavy workload without abandoning important read requirements?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q016](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q016)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q016](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q016)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How do write-heavy workloads change your indexing strategy?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Describe the change in priorities when writes dominate. Choose what to keep, alter or remove from the observed access patterns.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Balance write capacity with read service requirements through evidence.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State insert/update/delete proportions, important read paths and latency targets. Treat performance gains as hypotheses requiring representative load tests.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Identifies which indexes support important reads and which impose avoidable maintenance.</li>
<li>Validates both write behavior and read regressions rather than optimizing one metric.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Removing all indexes or keeping all of them without considering the workload contract.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What changes if writes arrive as a nightly batch instead of continuous traffic?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q011"></a>

### S03-Q011 · Production decision

<p>What evidence would justify creating an index, and how would you decide whether to keep it after deployment?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q011](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q011)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q011](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q011)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> When should you create an index?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Move from an observed access problem to a testable index proposal. Explain the acceptance and removal criteria for the change.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Make and validate an index decision across a representative workload.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use SQL Server with stated query frequency, data distribution and write load. An advisory suggestion or one plan is input, not the decision by itself.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Relates the key and coverage proposal to observed predicates and required columns.</li>
<li>Checks benefit, regressions and ongoing usage against an explicit baseline.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Creating every suggested index or deciding from a single fast local execution.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What would you measure if the target SELECT improves but API throughput falls?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>An ASP.NET Core order endpoint filters by tenant and time range while background workers insert new orders. Propose candidate indexes for a declared query and SQL Server deployment, compare representative distributions and explain how to test read benefits, write impact and the condition for rolling back the change. No benchmark result is supplied.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Explains index roles and proposes a plausible index for the query.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Defends key order and coverage from access needs, interprets actual evidence, and accepts or rejects the change based on both read and write requirements.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>No query, data distribution, plan or workload measurements are supplied; the candidate is not yet a demonstrated improvement.</p>
